name: Price incl. tax
description: Adds a tax rate to a base price, computing price×(1+rate/100). The result is the total amount payable including tax.
notes: Enter the tax rate as a percentage number (e.g. 10 for 10%), not as a fraction. The default rate is 10%.

name: Discounted price
description: Applies a discount to a price, computing price×(1−discount/100). The result is the amount paid after the discount is deducted.
notes: Enter the discount as a percentage number (e.g. 20 for 20%). A discount above 100 would give a negative, meaningless price.

name: Simple interest
description: Computes simple interest as principal×rate/100×years, the interest earned or owed when interest is not compounded.
notes: This is interest only, not principal plus interest. Rate is an annual percentage and years must use the same time period as the rate.

name: Compound total
description: The total of principal plus interest when a principal is invested at the annual rate (%) for the given number of years with compounding. Interest is added back to the principal and itself earns interest, so it grows faster than simple interest over long periods.
notes: Enter the rate as a percentage (5 for 5% per year, not 0.05). Assumes annual compounding; adjust the rate and count for semi-annual or monthly compounding. Taxes and fees are not included.

name: Loan monthly payment
description: Computes the fixed monthly repayment on an amortizing loan using principal×(mrate/100)/(1−(1+mrate/100)^(−months)). It spreads principal and interest evenly over the term.
notes: Rate is the monthly (not annual) percentage; divide an annual rate by 12. Months is the total number of payments. Assumes a fully amortizing fixed-rate loan.

name: Tip amount
description: Computes the gratuity as bill×rate/100, the tip amount to add based on the bill total and a chosen tip percentage.
notes: This returns only the tip, not the bill plus tip. Enter the rate as a percentage number; the default is 15%.

name: Compound interest amount
description: Computes the accumulated amount when a principal earns interest at an annual rate compounded n times per year over t years, using principal×(1 + r/n)^(n·t). The result is the total value at the end of the term.
notes: Enter the annual rate as a decimal, so 5 percent is 0.05. Increasing the compounding frequency n raises the final amount, but with diminishing effect.

name: Continuous compounding
description: Computes the amount grown by continuous compounding at an annual rate over t years, using principal×e^(r·t). It represents the limit of compounding an infinite number of times per year.
notes: Enter the rate as a decimal (5 percent is 0.05). For a given nominal rate, continuous compounding gives the highest possible accumulated value.

name: Future value (single sum)
description: Computes the future value of a single present sum after t periods growing at rate r per period, using present_value×(1 + r)^t. It shows what a lump sum today will be worth later.
notes: Enter r as a decimal per period, and keep r and t on the same period basis. This assumes a single deposit with no further contributions.

name: Present value (single sum)
description: Computes today's value of a single future sum received after t periods, discounted at rate r per period, using future_value/(1 + r)^t. It reverses compounding to find the equivalent amount now.
notes: Enter r as a decimal per period, matching the period of t. A higher discount rate or a longer horizon reduces the present value.

name: Future value of annuity
description: Computes the future value of a series of equal payments made each period at rate r for t periods, using payment×(((1 + r)^t − 1)/r). It totals what regular contributions grow to by the end.
notes: This assumes an ordinary annuity with payments at the end of each period and a constant rate. The rate r must not be zero; enter it as a decimal per period.

name: Present value of annuity
description: Computes the present value of a series of equal payments received each period at rate r for t periods, using payment×((1 − (1 + r)^(−t))/r). It sums the discounted worth of all future payments.
notes: This assumes an ordinary annuity with end-of-period payments and a constant rate that must not be zero. Enter r as a decimal per period matching t.

name: Effective annual rate
description: Computes the effective annual rate from a nominal rate r compounded n times per year, using (1 + r/n)^n − 1. It gives the true yearly return once compounding within the year is accounted for.
notes: Enter the nominal rate as a decimal; the result is also a decimal, so multiply by 100 for a percentage. The effective rate exceeds the nominal rate whenever n is greater than 1.

name: Rule of 72
description: Estimates the number of periods needed for an investment to double by dividing 72 by the growth rate expressed as a percent. It is a quick mental approximation of doubling time.
notes: Enter the rate as a percent number, so 6 percent is 6, not 0.06. It is an approximation most accurate for rates near 6 to 10 percent; use the exact doubling-time formula for precision.

name: CAGR
description: Computes the compound annual growth rate that takes a value from beginning to end over a number of years, using (ending/beginning)^(1/years) − 1. It is the constant yearly rate equivalent to the overall growth.
notes: The result is a decimal, so multiply by 100 for a percentage. It smooths out year-to-year variation and assumes the beginning value is positive.

name: Return on investment (ROI)
description: Computes the return on investment as the net gain divided by the cost, using (final_value − cost)/cost. It measures profit relative to the amount invested.
notes: The result is a decimal, so multiply by 100 for a percentage. It ignores how long the investment was held, so it is not directly an annual rate.

name: Gross margin
description: Computes the gross margin as revenue minus cost of goods sold, divided by revenue: (revenue − cogs)/revenue. It shows the fraction of sales left after direct production costs.
notes: The result is a decimal, so multiply by 100 for a percentage. It covers only cost of goods sold, not operating, tax, or other expenses.

name: Markup
description: Computes the markup as the selling price minus cost, divided by cost: (price − cost)/cost. It expresses profit as a fraction of the cost, the basis on which prices are set.
notes: Markup is measured against cost, whereas margin is measured against price, so the two differ. The result is a decimal; multiply by 100 for a percentage.

name: Break-even units
description: Computes the number of units that must be sold to cover fixed costs, using fixed/(price − varcost). At this quantity total revenue exactly equals total cost and profit is zero.
notes: The price per unit must exceed the variable cost per unit, or there is no positive break-even point. Fractional results are usually rounded up to whole units.

name: Break-even revenue
description: Computes the sales revenue needed to break even, using fixed×price/(price − varcost). It is the break-even number of units multiplied by the unit price.
notes: The unit price must exceed the variable cost per unit for a valid result. This gives revenue in currency, whereas break-even units gives a quantity.

name: Contribution margin ratio
description: Computes the contribution margin ratio as (price − varcost)/price, the share of each sales dollar left after variable costs. This portion goes toward covering fixed costs and profit.
notes: The result is a decimal, so multiply by 100 for a percentage. It reflects only variable costs per unit, not fixed costs.

name: Straight-line depreciation
description: Computes the annual depreciation expense of an asset spread evenly over its useful life, using (cost − salvage)/life. It allocates the same amount of cost to each year.
notes: The depreciable base is cost minus salvage value, and useful life is in years. This method assumes a constant charge, unlike accelerated depreciation schemes.

name: Net profit margin
description: Computes the net profit margin as net income divided by revenue. It shows the fraction of each sales dollar that remains as profit after all expenses and taxes.
notes: The result is a decimal, so multiply by 100 for a percentage. Unlike gross margin, this accounts for all costs including operating expenses, interest, and taxes.

name: NPV of single cash flow
description: Computes the net present value of one future cash flow against an initial investment, using cf/(1 + r)^t − c0. It discounts the future cash flow to today and subtracts the upfront cost.
notes: Enter the discount rate r as a decimal per period, matching the period of t. A positive result suggests the cash flow more than repays the initial investment.

name: Bond current yield
description: Computes a bond's current yield as its annual coupon payment divided by its current market price. It measures the income return relative to what the bond costs now.
notes: The result is a decimal, so multiply by 100 for a percentage. It reflects only coupon income and ignores any capital gain or loss at maturity, unlike yield to maturity.

name: Earnings per share (EPS)
description: Computes basic earnings per share by dividing a company's net income by the number of shares outstanding. The result shows how much profit is attributable to each share, a core measure of per-share profitability.
notes: Use the same period for income and shares. This basic EPS ignores dilution from options or convertibles; for preferred stock, subtract preferred dividends from net income first.

name: Dividend yield
description: Divides the annual dividend per share by the current share price to give the dividend yield. It expresses the cash return from dividends as a fraction of the price paid for the stock.
notes: Result is a fraction; multiply by 100 for a percentage. Use annualized dividends and a consistent currency. Yield rises as price falls, which can signal risk rather than value.

name: Gordon growth model
description: Estimates the fair value of a stock as next year's dividend divided by the required return minus the constant dividend growth rate. It values a share as the present value of dividends growing forever at a fixed rate.
notes: Required return must exceed the growth rate or the result is meaningless or negative. Rates are decimals (0.10 = 10%). Assumes perpetual, constant growth, so it suits stable dividend payers only.

name: Inflation-adjusted value
description: Converts a nominal future amount into today's purchasing power by discounting it with the inflation rate over the given number of years. The result is the real value after inflation erodes the money's worth.
notes: Inflation rate is a decimal per year (0.02 = 2%) and t is in years. Assumes a constant annual rate; it removes inflation, not investment discounting or taxes.

name: Real interest rate (Fisher)
description: Applies the exact Fisher equation to convert a nominal interest rate into a real rate, adjusting for inflation. It answers how much purchasing power actually grows after inflation is removed.
notes: Rates are decimals. This is the exact form; the common approximation real ≈ nominal − inflation drifts from this when rates are large. Result can be negative if inflation exceeds the nominal rate.

name: Currency conversion
description: Multiplies an amount in one currency by an exchange rate to obtain the equivalent value in another currency. The rate is the number of target-currency units per unit of the source currency.
notes: Make sure the rate is quoted in the intended direction (target per source); an inverted rate gives a very wrong figure. Real transactions also add spreads or fees not included here.

name: VAT amount
description: Calculates the value-added tax on a net (pre-tax) amount by multiplying it by the VAT rate. The result is the tax due, which is added to the net amount to reach the gross price.
notes: Applies to the net amount, not the gross. Rate is a decimal (0.10 = 10%). To back out VAT from a gross price instead, divide the gross by (1 + rate) first.

name: Sales tax amount
description: Computes the sales tax owed by multiplying a pre-tax price by the tax rate. The result is the added tax amount that a buyer pays on top of the listed price.
notes: Applies to the pre-tax price and rate is a decimal (0.10 = 10%). If a price already includes tax, this overstates the tax; extract it with price/(1 + rate) instead.

name: Payback period
description: Divides the initial investment by the annual cash flow to find the payback period, the number of years needed to recover the original outlay from equal yearly inflows.
notes: Assumes constant annual cash flow and ignores the time value of money and any inflows after payback. Use consistent currency for investment and cash flow.

name: Return on equity (ROE)
description: Divides net income by shareholder equity to measure return on equity, showing how much profit a company generates from each unit of owners' capital.
notes: Result is a fraction; multiply by 100 for a percentage. Use net income for the period and equity from the same basis; high leverage can inflate ROE without more efficiency.

name: Return on assets (ROA)
description: Divides net income by total assets to give return on assets, indicating how efficiently a company uses its assets to generate profit.
notes: Result is a fraction; multiply by 100 for a percentage. Use net income for the period; ROA varies widely across industries, so compare only within a sector.

name: Debt-to-equity ratio
description: Divides total debt by total equity to give the debt-to-equity ratio, a leverage measure showing how much borrowing a company uses relative to owners' capital.
notes: A ratio of 1 means debt equals equity. Definitions of debt vary (total liabilities vs. interest-bearing debt only), so state which is used when comparing companies.

name: Current ratio
description: Divides current assets by current liabilities to give the current ratio, a liquidity measure of a company's ability to cover short-term obligations with short-term assets.
notes: A ratio above 1 means current assets exceed current liabilities. Very high values may signal idle cash or excess inventory rather than strong liquidity.

name: Quick ratio
description: Subtracts inventory from current assets and divides by current liabilities to give the quick (acid-test) ratio, a stricter liquidity measure using only assets easily turned into cash.
notes: Inventory is excluded because it is hardest to liquidate quickly. A ratio of 1 means liquid assets just cover current liabilities; compare against the current ratio to gauge inventory reliance.

name: WACC
description: Computes the weighted average cost of capital by blending the cost of equity and the after-tax cost of debt according to their weights in the capital structure. It gives the overall required return that funds a firm's assets.
notes: Rates and weights are decimals, and the equity and debt weights should sum to 1. Only debt gets the (1 − tax) shield, reflecting the tax deductibility of interest.

name: Future Value of Ordinary Annuity
description: Computes the future value of an ordinary annuity, where equal payments are made at the end of each period. It sums each payment compounded at rate r over n periods using the annuity factor ((1+r)^n-1)/r.
notes: The rate r must match the payment period (e.g. monthly rate for monthly payments) and be entered as a decimal. Payments are assumed to occur at period end; use annuity due if paid at the start.

name: Present Value of Ordinary Annuity
description: Computes the present value of an ordinary annuity, discounting a series of equal end-of-period payments back to today at rate r over n periods. It gives the lump sum equivalent to the stream of payments.
notes: Enter r as a decimal per period matching the payment frequency. Payments are assumed at period end; the result grows as r falls toward zero.

name: Future Value of Annuity Due
description: Computes the future value of an annuity due, where equal payments are made at the beginning of each period. It equals the ordinary annuity future value multiplied by (1+r) because each payment earns one extra period of interest.
notes: Enter r as a decimal per period matching the payment frequency. Use this form only for beginning-of-period payments; it is always larger than the ordinary annuity value.

name: Present Value of Annuity Due
description: Computes the present value of an annuity due, where equal payments occur at the start of each period. It equals the ordinary annuity present value multiplied by (1+r) since each payment is discounted one period less.
notes: Enter r as a decimal per period matching the payment frequency. Applies only to beginning-of-period payments and is always larger than the ordinary annuity present value.

name: Perpetuity Present Value
description: Computes the present value of a perpetuity, an infinite stream of equal payments, as the payment divided by the discount rate. It gives the lump sum today worth of payments that continue forever.
notes: The rate r must be positive and entered as a decimal; the payment and rate must share the same period. The formula assumes constant, never-ending payments.

name: Growing Perpetuity Present Value
description: Computes the present value of a growing perpetuity, where payments grow at constant rate g each period forever, as the next payment divided by (r-g). It values an infinite, steadily rising cash flow stream.
notes: Requires the discount rate r to exceed the growth rate g, or the value diverges. Enter both as decimals; pmt is the payment one period from now, not today's.

name: Future Value of a Single Sum
description: Computes the future value of a single present amount compounded at rate r over n periods, as pv times (1+r)^n. It shows how much an investment today grows to with compound interest.
notes: The rate r must match the compounding period and be entered as a decimal. n is the number of compounding periods, not necessarily years.

name: Sinking Fund Payment
description: Computes the level periodic payment needed to accumulate a target future value fv over n periods at rate r, as fv times r/((1+r)^n-1). It is the deposit required each period to reach a savings goal.
notes: Enter r as a decimal per period matching the deposit frequency; payments are assumed at period end. It is the inverse of the future-value-of-annuity relationship.

name: Loan Balance After k Payments
description: Computes the outstanding loan balance after k payments as the compounded original principal minus the future value of the payments already made. It shows how much of the loan remains at a point in time.
notes: The rate r must be per payment period and entered as a decimal; k is the number of payments completed. Assumes a fixed payment and constant rate throughout.

name: Total Interest Paid on Loan
description: Computes the total interest paid over the life of a loan as the sum of all payments (payment times number of payments) minus the original principal. It shows the total cost of borrowing beyond the amount borrowed.
notes: Assumes a fully amortizing loan with a fixed payment for all n periods. It gives total interest only, excluding fees or charges; it is not a per-period figure.

name: Dividend Discount Model (Gordon Growth)
description: Estimates a stock's intrinsic value using the Gordon growth model as next year's dividend divided by (required return minus dividend growth rate). It values a share as a perpetuity of dividends growing at a constant rate.
notes: Requires the required return r to exceed the growth rate g, or the value is meaningless. Enter r and g as decimals; d is the dividend expected one year out.

name: PEG Ratio
description: Computes the price/earnings-to-growth (PEG) ratio by dividing the P/E ratio by the earnings growth rate expressed as a percentage. It adjusts the P/E for expected growth to gauge relative valuation.
notes: Here g is entered as a decimal and multiplied by 100 to become a percentage growth number. A PEG near 1 is often seen as fair value; g must be positive.

name: Earnings Yield
description: Computes the earnings yield as earnings per share divided by the share price, times 100 to give a percentage. It is the inverse of the P/E ratio and shows earnings generated per unit of price.
notes: Both EPS and price must use the same currency; the result is a percentage. It lets investors compare a stock's earnings return against bond yields or other assets.

name: Book Value per Share
description: Computes the book value per share as total assets minus total liabilities (shareholders' equity) divided by the number of shares outstanding. It gives the accounting net worth backing each share.
notes: This is a balance-sheet figure and may differ greatly from market price. Shares outstanding must be positive; it ignores intangible value and future earnings.

name: Price-to-Book Ratio
description: Divides the share price by book value per share to show how many times a stock trades above its accounting net worth. A result of 2 means the market values each share at twice its book equity per share.
notes: Book value per share reflects historical accounting equity, not market or liquidation value. Companies with heavy intangible assets or buybacks can show distorted or even negative book values.

name: Price-to-Sales Ratio
description: Divides total market capitalization by total revenue, showing how much investors pay for each unit of sales. A value of 2.5 means the market values the company at 2.5 times its annual revenue.
notes: Unlike P/E, this ignores profitability, so a low ratio does not imply a bargain if margins are poor. Compare only within the same industry, since typical sales multiples vary widely.

name: Enterprise Value
description: Adds total debt to market capitalization and subtracts cash to estimate the total cost of acquiring the whole business. It represents the takeover value available to all capital providers, not just equity holders.
notes: Cash is subtracted because an acquirer could use it to repay debt. Use market value of debt where available, and exclude only truly excess or non-operating cash for accuracy.

name: Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC)
description: Blends the cost of equity and the after-tax cost of debt, each weighted by its share of total financing, to give the firm's overall required return. It is the discount rate used to value the whole company.
notes: Weights should ideally use market values and sum to 1. The debt term is multiplied by (1 minus tax rate) to reflect the tax deductibility of interest; rates are entered as decimals.

name: Sharpe Ratio
description: Subtracts the risk-free rate from portfolio return and divides by the standard deviation of returns, measuring excess return earned per unit of total risk. Higher values indicate better risk-adjusted performance.
notes: Return and volatility must cover the same period (e.g. both annualized). It penalizes all volatility, including upside, and assumes roughly normal returns, so it can mislead for skewed strategies.

name: CAPM Expected Return
description: Uses the Capital Asset Pricing Model to estimate an asset's expected return as the risk-free rate plus beta times the market risk premium (market return minus risk-free rate). Beta scales how much market risk the asset carries.
notes: Enter all rates as decimals. Beta above 1 amplifies market moves and below 1 dampens them; the model assumes only systematic risk is rewarded and inputs are forward-looking estimates.

name: Bond Price
description: Values a bond as the present value of its coupon stream plus the discounted face value, using the yield per period. It sums an annuity of coupons and the lump-sum redemption discounted over n periods.
notes: Coupon, yield, and periods must all be on the same per-period basis (e.g. semiannual). Price rises when yield falls and falls when yield rises; the result is the fair present value at that yield.

name: Approximate Yield to Maturity
description: Estimates a bond's annual yield to maturity by adding the coupon to the annualized capital gain or loss, then dividing by the average of face value and price. The result is expressed as a percentage.
notes: This is an approximation that avoids solving the exact YTM equation, so it drifts from the true yield for large discounts or premiums and long maturities. Coupon and n are on an annual basis.

name: Holding Period Return
description: Combines price change and any income received over the holding period, divided by the starting price, to give the total percentage return earned while holding the asset.
notes: This is the total return for the whole period, not annualized, so it is not comparable across periods of different lengths. Income covers dividends, interest, or other cash distributions received.

name: Annualized Return
description: Converts a total holding period return into an equivalent compounded annual rate by taking the (1/years) root of one plus the total return and subtracting one. The result is a percentage per year.
notes: Enter the total return as a decimal (e.g. 0.5 for 50 percent). This assumes returns compound smoothly; it reflects the constant annual rate that produces the same cumulative growth.

name: Real Rate of Return
description: Adjusts a nominal return for inflation using the Fisher relation, dividing one plus the nominal rate by one plus inflation and subtracting one. The result is the inflation-adjusted return as a percentage.
notes: This exact form is more accurate than simply subtracting inflation from the nominal rate. Enter both rates as decimals; a negative result means purchasing power fell despite a positive nominal return.

name: After-Tax Return
description: Multiplies the pre-tax return by (1 minus the tax rate) to give the return an investor actually keeps after taxes, expressed as a percentage.
notes: Enter both the return and tax rate as decimals. This assumes the whole return is taxed at a single flat rate and ignores timing, deferral, and differing rates on income versus capital gains.

name: Compound Annual Rate from Total Return
description: Computes the compound annual growth rate (CAGR) from a total return over several years by taking the (1/years) root of one plus the total return and subtracting one. The result is a percentage per year.
notes: Enter total return as a decimal (e.g. 1.0 means the value doubled). CAGR smooths out volatility into a single constant annual rate and says nothing about the path taken between start and end.

name: Doubling Time (Rule of 69.3)
description: Estimates how many periods it takes for an investment to double at a given growth rate, dividing 69.3 by the rate expressed as a percentage. It approximates the exact log-based doubling time.
notes: The 69.3 constant (100 times ln 2) suits continuous or frequent compounding; the familiar Rule of 72 is a rougher variant. Enter the rate as a decimal, since the formula multiplies it by 100.

name: Present Value of Growing Annuity
description: Discounts a stream of payments that grow at a constant rate each period back to today, given the first payment, discount rate, growth rate, and number of periods. It sums the present value of all growing payments.
notes: Requires the discount rate to differ from the growth rate, since r minus g is a divisor. Payments are assumed at period end and each grows by g; enter all rates as decimals.

name: Future Value of Growing Annuity
description: Computes the accumulated value at the end of n periods of payments that grow at a constant rate, given the first payment, period rate, and growth rate. It totals each grown payment compounded to the final period.
notes: The rate per period must differ from the growth rate, as r minus g is the divisor. Payments are assumed at period end; enter rate and growth as decimals.

name: Net Present Value (2 Periods)
description: Discounts two years of cash flows back to today and subtracts the initial investment, giving the net present value of a simple project. A positive result means the project adds value at the given discount rate.
notes: Cash flows are assumed to arrive at the end of years 1 and 2, and the initial investment occurs now (time zero). Enter the discount rate as a decimal; this two-period form only handles c1 and c2.

name: Profitability Index
description: Divides the present value of a project's future cash flows by its initial investment, showing the value created per unit of money invested. A value above 1 indicates the project is expected to add value.
notes: The numerator should already be discounted to present value. A PI above 1 corresponds to a positive NPV; it is useful for ranking projects when capital is limited.

name: Price/Earnings Ratio
description: Divides the share price by earnings per share to show how much investors pay for each unit of earnings. A P/E of 20 means the market pays 20 times the company's annual per-share earnings.
notes: The ratio is undefined or meaningless when earnings are zero or negative. It depends on whether trailing or forward EPS is used, and should be compared within the same industry.

name: Dividend Payout Ratio
description: Divides total dividends by net income and multiplies by 100 to show the percentage of earnings paid out to shareholders as dividends. The remainder is reinvested in the business.
notes: The result becomes meaningless if net income is zero or negative. A payout above 100 percent means dividends exceed current earnings and are being funded from reserves or debt.

name: Retention Ratio
description: Calculates the share of net income kept in the business rather than paid out, as one minus the dividend payout ratio, expressed as a percentage. It is the plowback rate that funds internal growth.
notes: This is the complement of the payout ratio, so the two sum to 100 percent. Net income must be positive for a meaningful result; a higher retention rate supports reinvestment over distributions.

name: Sustainable Growth Rate
description: Multiplies return on equity by the retention ratio (one minus the payout ratio) to estimate how fast a firm can grow using only retained earnings, without new equity. The result is a percentage per year.
notes: Enter ROE and payout as decimals. It assumes constant margins, asset use, and leverage, and no new share issuance; growing faster generally requires external financing.

name: Interest Coverage Ratio
description: Divides earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) by interest expense to show how many times operating profit covers interest payments. A value of 8 means EBIT is eight times the interest owed.
notes: A higher ratio signals a greater cushion for servicing debt; values near or below 1 warn that operating profit barely covers interest. Interest must be positive for the ratio to be meaningful.

name: Treynor Ratio
description: Divides portfolio excess return (return minus the risk-free rate) by the portfolio's beta, measuring excess return earned per unit of systematic market risk. Higher values indicate better reward for market risk taken.
notes: Unlike the Sharpe ratio, it uses beta rather than total volatility, so it only credits systematic risk and suits well-diversified portfolios. Enter returns as decimals.

name: Jensen's Alpha
description: Measures a portfolio's excess return over the return predicted by CAPM for its beta. A positive alpha means the portfolio outperformed its risk-adjusted benchmark; zero means it earned exactly its expected return.
notes: Beta must reflect the portfolio's true market sensitivity, and all returns are entered as decimals over the same period. Alpha attributes skill only after accounting for systematic market risk.

name: Equivalent Annual Cost (Capital Recovery)
description: Converts a present-value cost into a level annual payment over n periods using the capital recovery factor, given the present value and period rate. It spreads a lump-sum cost into equal yearly amounts.
notes: Useful for comparing assets with different lifespans on an annual basis. Payments are assumed at period end; enter the rate as a decimal, and the result carries the same currency as the present value.

name: Continuous Compounding Future Value
description: Grows a present value forward using continuous compounding, multiplying it by e raised to the rate times time. It gives the future value when interest is compounded an infinite number of times per year.
notes: This yields a slightly higher value than discrete annual compounding at the same stated rate. Enter the rate as a decimal, and keep rate and time on the same time unit (typically years).

name: Free Cash Flow to Firm
description: Computes cash available to all investors by taking after-tax operating profit (EBIT times one minus tax), adding back depreciation, and subtracting capital expenditure and the increase in net working capital.
notes: Depreciation is added back because it is a non-cash expense already deducted in EBIT. Enter the tax rate as a decimal; nwc is the change in working capital, not its level.

name: Gross Profit Margin
description: Subtracts cost of goods sold from revenue, divides by revenue, and multiplies by 100 to show the percentage of sales remaining after direct production costs. It measures core production profitability.
notes: This covers only direct costs of goods sold, not operating, interest, or tax expenses. Revenue must be positive; compare within an industry since typical margins vary by sector.

name: Operating Margin
description: Divides operating income by revenue and multiplies by 100 to show the percentage of each sales dollar left after operating expenses. It gauges profitability from core operations, before interest and taxes.
notes: Operating income excludes interest and tax but includes overhead beyond direct costs, so it sits below gross margin. Revenue must be positive for a meaningful percentage.

name: Cash Ratio
description: Adds cash and marketable securities and divides by current liabilities, measuring the firm's ability to cover short-term obligations using only its most liquid assets. A value of 0.72 means liquid assets cover 72 percent of current liabilities.
notes: This is the strictest liquidity ratio, excluding receivables and inventory. A very high value may signal idle cash; current liabilities must be positive for a meaningful result.

name: Working Capital
description: Subtracts current liabilities from current assets to show the short-term liquid capital available to fund day-to-day operations. A positive figure means current assets exceed obligations due within a year.
notes: This is an absolute amount, not a ratio, so scale it against firm size when comparing. Negative working capital can indicate liquidity stress or, in some business models, efficient supplier financing.

name: Debt Ratio
description: Divides total debt by total assets to show the proportion of a company's assets financed by debt. A value of 0.44 means 44 percent of assets are funded through borrowing rather than equity.
notes: A higher ratio means greater financial leverage and risk. Definitions of debt vary (total liabilities versus interest-bearing debt only), so confirm which is used before comparing firms.

name: Equity Multiplier
description: Divides total assets by total equity to measure how much of the firm's assets are supported by each unit of shareholder equity. A value of 1.8 means assets are 1.8 times equity, with the rest funded by liabilities.
notes: It is a leverage measure: higher values mean more debt financing and greater risk. Equity must be positive; negative equity makes the multiplier meaningless.

name: Return on Capital Employed (ROCE)
description: Divides EBIT by capital employed (total assets minus current liabilities) and multiplies by 100, showing operating profit generated per unit of long-term capital. It measures how efficiently capital produces returns.
notes: Uses pre-interest, pre-tax profit so it is independent of financing structure. Capital employed must be positive; compare over time or against peers as absolute levels vary by industry.

name: Asset Turnover
description: Divides revenue by total assets to show how many units of sales the firm generates per unit of assets. A value of 0.56 means each dollar of assets produces 56 cents of revenue.
notes: Higher turnover signals more efficient use of assets to generate sales. It varies widely by industry, so compare only among similar businesses; ideally use average assets over the period.

name: Inventory Turnover
description: Divides cost of goods sold by average inventory to show how many times inventory is sold and replaced over the period. A value of 4 means stock cycles through roughly four times per year.
notes: Using COGS (not revenue) keeps numerator and denominator on a cost basis. Higher turnover suggests efficient inventory management, but too high may risk stockouts; average inventory must be positive.

name: Days Inventory Outstanding (DIO)
description: Multiplies average inventory by 365 and divides by cost of goods sold to estimate the average number of days inventory is held before being sold. Lower values mean stock moves faster.
notes: It is the inverse of inventory turnover expressed in days and assumes a 365-day year. Use average inventory and match COGS to the same period for accuracy.

name: Receivables Turnover
description: Divides revenue by average accounts receivable to show how many times the firm collects its receivables over the period. A value of 8.33 means receivables are collected roughly eight times per year.
notes: Higher turnover indicates faster collection of credit sales. Ideally use credit sales rather than total revenue, and average receivables; the denominator must be positive.

name: Days Sales Outstanding (DSO)
description: Multiplies average receivables by 365 and divides by revenue to estimate the average number of days it takes to collect payment after a sale. Lower values mean cash is collected sooner.
notes: It is the inverse of receivables turnover in days and assumes a 365-day year. For accuracy use credit sales and average receivables matched to the same period.

name: Payables Turnover
description: Divides cost of goods sold by average accounts payable to show how many times the firm pays off its suppliers over the period. A value of 6.67 means payables are settled roughly seven times per year.
notes: A higher ratio means faster payment to suppliers; a lower one means the firm holds cash longer. Use purchases or COGS consistently, and average payables; the denominator must be positive.

name: Days Payables Outstanding (DPO)
description: Multiplies average payables by 365 and divides by cost of goods sold to estimate the average number of days the firm takes to pay its suppliers. Higher values mean the firm holds onto cash longer.
notes: It is the inverse of payables turnover in days and assumes a 365-day year. Longer DPO improves cash flow but stretching too far may strain supplier relationships; match COGS to the period.

name: Cash Conversion Cycle
description: Adds days inventory outstanding and days sales outstanding, then subtracts days payables outstanding, to show how many days cash is tied up between paying suppliers and collecting from customers.
notes: A shorter or negative cycle means cash is freed up faster or suppliers effectively finance operations. All three inputs must be measured over the same period and in days.

name: Contribution Margin (per unit)
description: Subtracts the variable cost per unit from the selling price to show how much each unit sold contributes toward covering fixed costs and profit. A value of 20 means each sale adds 20 toward fixed costs.
notes: This covers only variable costs, not fixed costs, so a positive margin does not yet mean profit. Both inputs must be per single unit and in the same currency.

name: Margin of Safety
description: Subtracts break-even sales from actual sales, divides by actual sales, and multiplies by 100 to show how far sales can fall before reaching break-even. A value of 50 percent means sales could halve before a loss.
notes: A larger margin means more buffer against a downturn. Actual sales must be positive and above break-even for a positive result; both should be measured over the same period.

name: Degree of Operating Leverage
description: Divides total contribution margin by operating income to measure how sensitive operating profit is to changes in sales. A value of 2.2 means a 1 percent change in sales moves operating income by about 2.2 percent.
notes: Higher leverage means larger fixed costs and greater profit volatility in both directions. Operating income must be positive; the measure applies near the current sales level, not for large jumps.

name: Diluted EPS
description: Subtracts preferred dividends from net income and divides by the diluted share count, giving earnings per share assuming all convertible securities and options are exercised. It shows the most conservative per-share earnings.
notes: The diluted share count includes potential shares from options, warrants, and convertibles, so diluted EPS is at or below basic EPS. Preferred dividends are removed because they belong to preferred, not common, holders.

name: Price-to-Earnings (P/E) Ratio
description: Divides the price per share by earnings per share to show how much investors pay for each unit of earnings. A P/E of about 27 means the market pays 27 times the company's per-share earnings.
notes: The ratio is undefined or meaningless when EPS is zero or negative, and depends on trailing versus forward earnings. Compare within an industry, since typical multiples differ across sectors.

name: EBITDA Margin
description: Divides EBITDA by revenue and multiplies by 100 to show operating profitability before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, as a percentage of sales. A value of 26 percent means EBITDA is 26 percent of revenue.
notes: By excluding depreciation and amortization it approximates operating cash generation but ignores capital intensity and financing. Revenue must be positive; compare within an industry.

name: Times Interest Earned
description: Reconstructs EBIT by adding tax and interest expense back to net income, then divides by interest expense to show how many times pre-tax operating profit covers interest. A value of 5 means EBIT is five times the interest owed.
notes: Adding tax and interest back to net income rebuilds EBIT so the numerator is on a pre-interest, pre-tax basis. Interest expense must be positive; a value near 1 signals thin coverage.

name: Fixed Asset Turnover
description: Divides revenue by net fixed assets to measure how efficiently a company uses its plant, property and equipment to generate sales. A result of 1.56 means each currency unit of net fixed assets produces 1.56 units of revenue.
notes: Net fixed assets means value after accumulated depreciation. Higher is generally better, but norms vary by industry, so compare only within the same sector.

name: Gross Margin from Markup
description: Converts a markup (profit as a fraction of cost) into gross margin (profit as a percent of selling price) via markup/(1+markup)×100. A 0.5 markup corresponds to a 33.33% gross margin.
notes: Markup is entered as a fraction, not a percent, so 50% markup is 0.5. Markup and margin are not the same figure; markup always exceeds the equivalent margin.

name: Markup from Margin
description: Converts a gross margin (profit as a fraction of selling price) into the equivalent markup on cost via margin/(1-margin)×100. A 0.3 margin corresponds to a 42.86% markup.
notes: Margin is entered as a fraction between 0 and 1, not a percent. As margin approaches 1 the required markup rises steeply toward infinity.

name: Selling Price from Cost & Margin
description: Computes the selling price needed to achieve a target gross margin from a unit cost, using cost/(1-margin). At a cost of 100 and a 0.4 target margin the price is 166.67.
notes: Margin is a fraction of the selling price, not of cost, and must be below 1. Simply adding the margin percentage to cost would understate the required price.

name: Sell-through Rate
description: Expresses the percentage of received inventory that was sold within a period, as units sold divided by units received times 100. Selling 180 of 300 received units gives a 60% sell-through rate.
notes: Both counts should cover the same period and product. A rate near 100% may signal understocking, while a low rate suggests overstock or weak demand.

name: Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)
description: Divides total marketing and sales spending by the number of new customers acquired to find the average cost of gaining one customer. Spending 50000 to gain 250 customers yields a CAC of 200 per customer.
notes: Include all marketing and sales costs for the period, and count only genuinely new customers. Compare against customer lifetime value to judge whether acquisition is profitable.

name: Customer Lifetime Value (LTV)
description: Estimates the total revenue one customer generates over their relationship, as average order value times purchases per year times average lifespan in years. Here 120×4×3 gives an LTV of 1440.
notes: This simple form uses revenue and ignores gross margin, discounting and retention decay, so it tends to overstate true profit-based lifetime value.

name: LTV to CAC Ratio
description: Divides customer lifetime value by customer acquisition cost to show how much value each acquired customer returns per unit of acquisition spend. An LTV of 1440 against a CAC of 200 gives a ratio of 7.2.
notes: A common health benchmark is around 3 or higher; a very high ratio may indicate underinvestment in growth. Use consistent LTV and CAC definitions (both revenue or both margin based).

name: Churn Rate
description: Gives the percentage of customers lost during a period, as customers lost divided by customers at the start times 100. Losing 50 of 1000 starting customers is a 5% churn rate.
notes: The denominator is the count at the start of the period, and new customers gained during the period are excluded. Retention rate is 100 minus this value.

name: Conversion Rate
description: Expresses the share of visitors who completed a desired action, as conversions divided by visitors times 100. With 320 conversions from 8000 visitors the conversion rate is 4%.
notes: Define a conversion consistently (purchase, signup, etc.) and count unique visitors over the same window to avoid inflating or deflating the rate.

name: Average Order Value (AOV)
description: Divides total revenue by the number of orders to find the average amount spent per order. Revenue of 96000 across 800 orders gives an AOV of 120.
notes: Use the same period for both figures and decide consistently whether revenue includes tax, shipping and refunds, since that changes the result.

name: Return on Ad Spend (ROAS)
description: Divides revenue attributed to advertising by the amount spent on those ads to show revenue earned per unit of ad spend. Revenue of 120000 on 30000 of spend gives a ROAS of 4.
notes: ROAS is a revenue ratio, not profit; it ignores product cost and margins, so a ROAS above 1 does not guarantee overall profitability.

name: Cost per Mille (CPM)
description: Gives the advertising cost per one thousand impressions, as ad cost divided by impressions times 1000. A cost of 4500 over 900000 impressions is a CPM of 5.
notes: Mille means one thousand, hence the ×1000 scaling. CPM measures cost of reach only and says nothing about clicks or conversions.

name: Cost per Click (CPC)
description: Divides advertising cost by the number of clicks to find the average price paid for each click. Spending 4500 for 3000 clicks gives a CPC of 1.50.
notes: CPC covers clicks only, not conversions or sales, so a low CPC is not automatically efficient if those clicks do not convert.

name: Price-to-Book (P/B) Ratio
description: Divides a stock's market price per share by its book value per share to show how the market values the firm relative to its net accounting assets. A price of 30 over book value 9 gives a P/B of 3.33.
notes: Book value uses accounting figures and can differ greatly from real asset worth, especially for asset-light or intangible-heavy firms. Typical levels vary by industry.

name: Operating Cash Flow Ratio
description: Divides operating cash flow by current liabilities to measure how well cash generated from operations covers short-term obligations. A ratio of 1.2 means operations produced 1.2 times the current liabilities in cash.
notes: A ratio above 1 indicates operating cash alone can meet current liabilities. It uses actual cash flow, so it is less exposed to accrual accounting distortions than the current ratio.

name: Loan-to-Value Ratio
description: Computes the loan-to-value (LTV) ratio as the loan amount divided by the appraised property value, times 100. Lenders use this percentage to gauge risk when underwriting a mortgage.
notes: Loan amount and property value must be in the same currency. A lower LTV generally means less lender risk and can qualify a borrower for better rates.

name: Break-even Ratio
description: Divides the break-even sales level by actual sales and multiplies by 100 to show what percentage of current sales is needed just to cover costs. A lower ratio indicates a larger safety margin above break-even.
notes: Both figures must be in the same currency and period. A ratio above 100% means actual sales have not yet reached break-even.

name: Gross Rental Yield
description: Computes gross rental yield as annual rental income divided by the property purchase price, times 100. It is a simple, unadjusted measure of a rental property's income return.
notes: This ignores operating expenses, vacancy, and financing costs; use net rental yield for a more complete picture. Income and price must be in the same currency.

name: Net Rental Yield
description: Subtracts annual operating expenses from annual rental income, divides by the property price, and multiplies by 100 to give net rental yield. It reflects the return after the costs of running the property.
notes: Operating expenses typically include maintenance, insurance, management fees, and taxes, but not mortgage interest. All figures must share the same currency and period.
